A nested call argument went from 7 frames to 3 ... The corpus model puts the peak at ≈78 frames before and ≈51 after, which leaves ≈13 frames ... of headroom'.

expectations.text: Architecture and performance findings come before correctness, test or commit-message findings in the review's ordering.

Every ARCH and PERF finding precedes every test, correctness and commit-message item.

expectations.text: The review does not recommend splitting functions for length or adding defensive checks.
expectations.evidence: No length-based splitting. 'What I would leave alone' keeps the folds: 'Folding ParsePostfix into ParseUnary and ParseArgument into ParseArguments. The recommended 'if (c.failed) { return -1; }' guard skips discarded failure-path work and isn't a defensive check against invalid state.

claims.evidence: Not verifiable without running the fixture. The review labels it a model estimate and lists measuring it under 'What I would measure'.

suggestions.assertion: The review identifies that the change reshapes the parser to fit the VM's call-depth limit and treats it as an architecture issue, with a number (the limit, a depth count or the remaining headroom).
suggestions.reason: Quoting the limit (64) satisfies this, and the commit's own context makes it easy to find, so both configurations pass. Ask for the measured or estimated headroom or the per-level frame cost to make it discriminate.

suggestions.assertion: The review proposes a concrete alternative or target shape for that workaround (for example raising the limit, a different iteration structure, or restoring the removed procedures after a limit change).
suggestions.reason: Both runs pass. 'Raise the limit and restore the procedures' is the obvious answer once the limit is identified, so this adds little beyond the previous assertion.

suggestions.assertion: The review does not recommend splitting functions for length or adding defensive checks.
suggestions.reason: Both runs recommend 'if (c.failed) { return -1; }' at the top of Expect, a work-skipping early-out that a grader could read as a defensive check. The baseline fails here only because it cites the small-functions rule. Define 'defensive check' (a guard against an invalid state that should be an assert) so the outcome doesn't depend on reading that guard.

No assertion covers either of the two configuration-unique correctness findings. Only the with-skill run found the int overflow in 'int budget = (int)(size * STEPS_PER_BYTE) + 100000' (source_parser_chibi.c:85, overflows above 357,897 bytes while MAX_SOURCE is 524,288). Only the baseline found that language-source-parser-chibi and language-source-tokenizer-chibi are in no tools/test_policy.py group. Add assertions for both.

Neither the pre-existing Differ double Build (SourceParserDiff.chibi:10,21) nor the commit silently fixing a red parent is asserted. Both runs noticed the red parent, so that one wouldn't discriminate, but the double Build is a with-skill-only perf finding.

eval_feedback.overall: The quantification (A3, A5) and ordering (A4) assertions discriminate well. A1 and A2 pass for both and mostly re-test the same insight. A6 hinges on an interpretation of 'defensive checks' and 'for length' that should be made explicit.
